opus-5.5.text:
I think the progress has been really impressive, honestly. If you look at the past couple of years, Chinese teams have gone from being seen as fast followers to producing models that are genuinely at or near the frontier on many benchmarks. Groups like DeepSeek, Qwen from Alibaba, Kimi from Moonshot, and others have shown that you can get very strong results with a lot of engineering discipline and efficiency. DeepSeek in particular made the whole world rethink how much compute you really need to train a competitive model — the work on mixture-of-experts, on efficient attention, on reinforcement learning for reasoning, that was very creative.

The other thing I really appreciate is the open-weight culture. Many of the strongest Chinese models are released openly, and that has a huge impact on the research community globally. At NVIDIA, and in academia, people build on top of these models every day. That openness accelerates everyone.

From my own perspective — I work mostly on generative models for visual content and on physical AI, world models, things like Cosmos — I see Chinese teams also moving very quickly in video generation and multimodal models. Some of the video models coming out of China are among the best in the world in terms of visual quality and motion.

Where I think the next challenge lies, for everyone, not just China, is going beyond language and pixels into the physical world. Robots, autonomous vehicles, embodied agents — they need models that understand physics, causality, 3D space. That requires different kinds of data and different kinds of evaluation. China has a big advantage there in manufacturing and hardware ecosystems, so I'm quite optimistic we'll see a lot of strong work in physical AI coming from there as well.

So overall, my assessment is: very strong, very fast, very efficient, and contributing a lot to the open ecosystem. Competition and collaboration together are pushing the whole field forward.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think China's current generation of models is genuinely strong, and I say that as someone who looks at this from the inside of the industry rather than from the outside.

If you look at the open-weight ecosystem over the past two years, a lot of the momentum has come from Chinese teams. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, MiniMax, and others have shown that you can get to near-frontier quality with far less compute than people assumed was necessary. That changed the conversation globally. It forced everyone, including us in the US, to think harder about efficiency, about mixture-of-experts design, about training recipes, and about how much of the gap was really about hardware versus engineering discipline.

I would highlight a few things. First, the engineering talent is excellent. The systems work, the optimization of inference, the willingness to publish detailed technical reports, that is real and it benefits the whole field. Second, the open approach has given Chinese models enormous reach. Developers everywhere are building on them because they are good and because they are accessible. That is a form of influence that is easy to underestimate.

At the same time, I would be honest about the constraints. Compute access is still the main bottleneck. The models are efficient partly because they have to be, and efficiency can compensate for a lot, but at the very top of the frontier scale still matters, especially for the next phase, which I think is less about chat and more about reasoning, agents, and physical AI, meaning models that understand and act in the real world. Those directions are extremely data- and compute-hungry. Video world models, robotics foundation models, simulation at scale, these are areas where I spend most of my time, and the gap there is still meaningful.

The other thing I watch is the move from catching up to defining new directions. Chinese labs have proven they can match and sometimes beat existing benchmarks. The harder question is who sets the next paradigm. I see early signs that Chinese teams are starting to do that, particularly in efficient training and in multimodal work, and the robotics ecosystem in China, with its manufacturing base, is a real structural advantage for physical AI.

So my overall assessment is: strong, fast-moving, underestimated for a long time and now perhaps slightly overcorrected in the other direction. The competition is healthy for the field. From where I sit, the more capable models there are, Chinese or American, the faster we all learn, and I'd rather be in a world where the frontier is being pushed from several places at once.

astra-6.text:
I would look at several dimensions rather than give a single ranking: model capability, efficiency, and how useful these systems are in practice. A model can perform well on benchmarks, but the harder question is whether it reliably solves problems for users.

For China’s current generation of AI models, I would want to examine those dimensions separately. How well do they reason through unfamiliar problems? How much computation do they need? And how consistently do they work outside a carefully controlled demonstration?

I’d also distinguish catching up on established tasks from introducing new ideas. Both are valuable, but they tell us different things about the development of an ecosystem. Without comparing specific models and evidence, I’d be cautious about making a broad claim that they are ahead or behind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there has been substantial progress, but I would separate a few dimensions. One is the capability of the models themselves: how well they reason, write code, understand images, and follow instructions. Another is efficiency: how much computation and cost it takes to deliver those capabilities. And then there is practical usefulness—whether people can reliably use these models to get work done.

When we discuss China’s current generation of models, I would be cautious about treating them as one group or reducing the assessment to a single ranking. Different teams can make different tradeoffs, and a strong benchmark result does not necessarily translate into a better product.

For me, the most interesting question is whether improvements are repeatable and broadly useful. Can a model handle unfamiliar problems? Can developers build on it easily? Can it deliver consistent results at a reasonable cost? Those are the things I would look at to judge the depth of the progress.
